notes.meaning: All the parts of the tabernacle were finished, but Moses did not set it up on his own. He waited until the LORD told him to. Henry says it is good to let God go before us in every step.

God picked New Year's Day for setting up the tabernacle, the tent where He would meet His people. This was almost exactly a year after Israel left Egypt. The building work had taken about six months. Henry draws a simple lesson: it is good to begin a new year by putting God first and serving Him better than before.

The ark came first. It was the gold-covered chest that held God's law, and it was the most precious object of all. As soon as it was in place it was hidden behind the veil, a thick curtain. The tabernacle had to be put together by God's pattern, just as it had been built by it.
Next came the table and the lampstand. To "set out its arrangement" means placing the twelve loaves of bread on the table in the way God had laid down. The lamps were also to be set up and lit.

The gold altar was where incense was burned. "In front of the ark" means just outside the veil, in the first room of the tent called the Holy Place. The curtain at the entrance hung between that room and the courtyard outside.

Outside the tent, in the courtyard, stood the big altar for burnt offerings and the water basin. Then the fence of curtains around the courtyard went up, with its own entrance curtain. Henry notes that everything had its proper place and order. With many hands helping, it could all be done in one day.

Moses was to pour special oil on the tent and everything in it. This would "consecrate" them, which means set them apart for God's use alone. Calvin and others say the oil itself had no power; it was a picture of the Holy Spirit, who makes things holy. Keil explains that the altar is called "most holy" because it stood out in the open where people came near it. Calvin links that title to the sacrifices offered on it.

Aaron, the high priest, was to be washed, dressed in holy clothes, and anointed with oil. Then he could begin serving God. Henry says those who serve at God's house must be clean. He adds that this high priesthood stayed in Aaron's family until Christ came, who is our high priest forever.

Aaron's sons were also dressed and anointed as priests. Their anointing was simpler, because oil was poured only on the high priest's head. This first anointing counted for all the ordinary priests who came after them. The Geneva Notes and Clarke say this priesthood was meant to last until Christ, the true High Priest, came.
Moses obeyed every command, and he did things in the order God set. Keil notes that this verse sums up the whole job. The anointing of the priests actually happened a little later (Leviticus 8).

The tabernacle went up on the first day of Israel's second year out of Egypt. Calvin points out how carefully Moses followed God's plan, not changing even small details. He warns that people are quick to mix their own ideas into God's commands.

Moses built the frame first. He laid the bases, stood up the wooden frames, and slid in the crossbars. Then he laid the cloth and the layers of animal-skin covering over the top, since the tent had no other roof. The words "just as the LORD had commanded" now begin to repeat. They appear seven times in this short passage.

"The Testimony" means the two stone tablets with the Ten Commandments. Moses put them in the ark, added the carrying poles, and set the gold lid called the mercy seat on top. Then he carried the ark into the back room and hung the veil to hide it.
The table went on the north side of the first room, outside the veil. Moses set the bread on it right away. Henry says God will never have His table left empty.

The lampstand stood across from the table, on the south side, and Moses lit its lamps. Ellicott says they were lit at the proper time, in the evening. Henry notes that God did not want unlit lamps in His house.

The gold altar went in the middle, right in front of the veil, and Moses burned sweet incense on it. Henry sees a lesson in how Moses used each new item at once. God's gifts are meant to be used, not just admired.
Moses hung the curtain at the door of the tent. It separated the holy room inside from the courtyard outside.

The big altar stood in the courtyard in line with the tent's door. Moses offered the burnt offering and grain offering on it. Keil takes this to be the daily morning and evening offering. Henry thinks Moses was starting the dedication service, which took seven days to finish, and then handed the work to the priests.

The basin of water stood between the altar and the tent. The priests washed their hands and feet there every time they went in or came to the altar. God wanted service from clean hands. Some say Moses showed how by washing there himself. Others take verses 31-32 as a note about how the basin was used from then on.

With the courtyard fence and gate in place, the job was done. This completed God's command to build a holy place so He could live among His people (Exodus 25:8). JFB thinks the people were probably gathered all around to watch, though the text does not say so.

The cloud that had led Israel came down on the tent, and God's glory filled it. This glory is sometimes called the Shekinah, meaning God's presence made visible. God had made the world and then put man in it; now Moses had made the tent and God moved in. It showed that God accepted their work and had brought back His favor after the golden calf.

The glory was so bright and awesome that even Moses could not go in. The same thing happened when Solomon's temple was dedicated (1 Kings 8:10-11). Henry and JFB say this shows how weak even the best people are before God. They add that Jesus has gone in for us and invites us to come boldly to God.

The cloud now told Israel when to travel. When it lifted, they packed up and moved. When it stayed, they stayed. Calvin notes that the cloud did not follow a fixed routine; sometimes it stayed a long time, sometimes it moved often. That showed God's fatherly care for His people.

By day a cloud, and by night fire, rested over the tent where everyone could see it. It stayed through all their journeys until they reached the promised land. Henry and JFB compare it to the Bible, God's sure guide for the church today. Clarke also sees in it the Holy Spirit, who leads God's people every step of life.
